clue.text: Tearing off, one offers no thanks

indicators.note: something gone off is spoilt and out of shape, so the word before it is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, all seven letters

explanation.surface: Someone rips open a present and walks off without a word of gratitude.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrate is an ungrateful person, one who never says thank you for a favour.

clue.text: One stunner captivating male in charge

indicators.note: captivating literally means taking captive, so the outer pieces hold the next one inside

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
a peach is an attractive person, a stunner
M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A beautiful woman has captured the heart of the man in command.
explanation.walkthrough: The male letter goes between the one and the stunner, inside the pair they make together.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach is to accuse formally of wrongdoing, a verb synonym of charge.

clue.text: A delay over staging opening night?

indicators.note: in a down clue over means turned upside down, so the first two words read backwards

blocks.note: a lag is a delay
a staging of a play is a performance of it

explanation.surface: A hold-up during the production delays the premiere.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as an example: an opening night is often, not always, a gala show.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala performance is a special festive showing, such as a premiere or first night.

clue.text: Vegetable's heart, OK chopped up, served about one, cold

indicators.note: chopping up cuts into bits that fall in any order, so the letters are rearranged
served about means placed around, so the jumbled letters surround the last two pieces

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
C for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A recipe: the heart of a vegetable, chopped, served around something cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart' looks like part of the vegetable, as in artichoke heart, but it is only anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The artichoke is a thistle-like plant whose flower bud is eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Odds still short

blocks.note: even as an adverb means still, as in even better
S as an abbreviation for short

explanation.walkthrough: Short is shortened to its initial S; 'still' works as in 'even more', not as calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Evens are betting odds of one to one, where a winning stake is doubled.

clue.text: Trade — fine one in craft at sea

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and adrift, so the letters of the vessel word get rearranged
placed in means the first pair of pieces sit inside the reworked letters

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A boat at sea is fined for some dodgy trade, perhaps smuggling.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion lands after the fourth letter of the rearranged vessel, not at its centre; 'craft' and 'trade' sit naturally together, hiding which is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic as a noun is commerce or dealing in goods, often illicit, so it is a synonym of trade.

clue.text: Where she will appear, given the right case?

definitions.text: Where she will appear, given the right case?

blocks.note: surface reading: where some woman will turn up
setter's reading: with a capital letter, 'She' is the novel by Rider Haggard, whose name is printed at the front of the book

explanation.walkthrough: In upper case 'She' is H. Rider Haggard's novel; the page at the front of a book shows its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The page at the start of a book bearing its name and author is where a capitalised 'She' would appear.

clue.text: A well-bred fellow envoy

blocks.note: taken as written
gent is short for gentleman, a well-bred man

explanation.surface: An ambassador who is a gentleman of good breeding.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent is someone acting on behalf of another, as an envoy acts for a government.

clue.text: The way a baby eats in poverty?

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: food is lifted by fingers to the lips
second meaning: living with nothing to spare, spending everything as soon as it comes

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a precarious existence with no savings, while literally describing a toddler feeding itself.

clue.text: Dilapidated car left in outskirts of city, at little cost

indicators.note: in says the vehicle and the direction go inside the boundary letters
outskirts are the edges of a town, so only the outside letters of the place are used

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
a heap is slang for an old, rundown car
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: An old banger left on the edge of town, bought for next to nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheaply means for a low price, inexpensively.

clue.text: Instruction to the trainee bell-ringer, 22?

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: a learner ringer is told which rope to tug next
second meaning: the answer to 22 across, an expression of disbelief

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom originally refers to leg-pulling: 'pull the other one, it's got bells on' means you are teasing me. Here it is read literally as a bell-ringing instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiomatic retort to an unbelievable claim, matching the other entry's exclamation of incredulity.

clue.text: A food flavouring chopped for a jelly

indicators.note: something chopped has had its end cut off, so the last letter of the flavouring goes

blocks.note: taken as written
spice is a food flavouring such as cinnamon or pepper

explanation.surface: A cook chops up a seasoning to put into a jelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a savoury jelly made from meat stock, used to set or glaze cold dishes.

clue.text: Two phases involved in piecework factory, perhaps

indicators.note: involved means tangled or intricate, so the letters of the two words are mixed together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Production in a piecework factory is split into two stages.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing 'perhaps' marks the definition as an example: a sweatshop is often, not always, paid by the piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweatshop is a workplace with poor conditions where workers are commonly paid per item made.

clue.text: Girl after harp, mostly, or mouth organ

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the instrument word loses its final letter
after places the girl's name behind the shortened instrument

blocks.note: taken as written, then cut short
a girl's name, as crosswords often require

explanation.surface: A girl takes up the harp, more or less, or else the mouth organ.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonica is a small wind instrument played with the lips, also called a mouth organ.

clue.text: Awkward choice associated with major sport

indicators.note: awkward suggests clumsy and ill-arranged, so the following word's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
a major is a musical key, as in C major

explanation.surface: A difficult decision about one of the big sports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'major' looks like an adjective for sport but it is the noun: a key such as A major.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice hockey is a team game played on ice with sticks and a puck.

clue.text: Crooked? It can get one by!

blocks.note: first meaning: bowed or curved, as of legs bent outwards
second meaning, cryptically

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads like advice about slipping past someone, but the answer splits as B AND Y, and those two letters together make 'by'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bandy describes legs that curve outward at the knee, so crooked or bowed is a fair synonym.

clue.text: A gun held by beautiful woman pointing at game

indicators.note: held by means gripped inside, so the beauty's letters wrap around the weapon

blocks.note: a belle is a beautiful woman
taken as written
gat is old American slang for a pistol

explanation.surface: A beautiful woman holds a gun and aims it at her quarry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' looks like hunted animals in the surface, but it is a pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Bagatelle is a table game in which balls are struck into holes guarded by pins.

clue.text: Bond actor getting extra round in

indicators.note: in tells us the circle-shaped piece goes inside the word for extra

blocks.note: more means additional, extra
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A James Bond star demands another round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Moore played James Bond in seven films from 1973 to 1985.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Moore is one of the actors who played 007, so the surname fits Bond actor.

clue.text: Pleasant to listen to, MC introduces eastern pop hero to the north

indicators.note: in a down clue going to the north means reading upwards, so the hero word is turned round
introduces means brings inside, so the two letters of the first piece enclose the rest

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for eastern
a pop idol is a music hero

explanation.surface: A master of ceremonies brings on a pop star from the East to sweet music.
explanation.definitionFit: Melodic means tuneful, having a pleasing melody.

clue.text: Greet nice comic, full of beans

indicators.note: comic means funny or absurd, so the preceding words are jumbled in a silly way

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Welcome a pleasant, lively comedian onto the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of beans is a British idiom for lively and bursting with vigour.

clue.text: Decrepit person failing to finish the fancy needlework

indicators.note: failing to finish means stopping short of the end, so the last letter is dropped
fancy means elaborate or fanciful, so the letters of the little word are rearranged

blocks.note: a crock is an old, worn-out person
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An old woman who cannot finish her fine sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy needlework' reads as a phrase, but 'fancy' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Crochet is handwork in which yarn is looped with a hooked needle into fabric.

clue.text: Old English beverage the sheep farmer helps to produce?

definitions.text: the sheep farmer helps to produce?

blocks.note: first meaning: a traditional drink of hot spiced ale with roasted apple pulp

blocks.clueFragment: the sheep farmer helps to produce?
blocks.note: second meaning: soft fine wool shorn from young sheep

explanation.walkthrough: The old drink was named for the fluffy apple pulp floating on the ale, which looked like fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the name of a historic wassail drink and the fine wool from young sheep.

clue.text: Simple chap's offence — gets short time inside

indicators.note: inside means the brief time piece goes within the offence word

blocks.note: a sin is a moral offence
mo is short for moment

explanation.surface: A simple-minded fellow's crime earns him a brief stretch in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Simple Simon is the nursery-rhyme character who met a pieman; 'short time' reads as a prison term.
explanation.definitionFit: The name completes the nursery rhyme figure Simple Simon, so a simple chap is that boy.

clue.text: I'm entering illuminated border

indicators.note: entering means going into, so the first word sits inside the next

blocks.note: lit means lighted up
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone stepping into a lit-up boundary area.
explanation.definitionFit: A limit is a boundary or edge, the line where something ends.

clue.text: Time for work happened upon after retirement?

indicators.note: retiring is going backwards, withdrawing, so the pieces are read right to left

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a work
to have met is to have come across

explanation.surface: A retired person spends their free time on a job they stumbled into.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is the speed or time of a piece of music, as in keeping time.

clue.text: Come off it! It's what the straight man may have said

definitions.text: It's what the straight man may have said

blocks.note: first meaning: an exclamation of disbelief

blocks.clueFragment: It's what the straight man may have said
blocks.note: second meaning, read literally: a stooge has no gags of his own and asks for none

explanation.walkthrough: The straight man in a comic double act feeds the lines; he never gets the laughs, so the phrase is read as his literal request.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiomatic retort meaning that what was said is ridiculous, just as 'come off it' is.

clue.text: A NY cell disposed of without difficulty

indicators.note: disposed can mean arranged or set out, so the letters are set out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A New York prison cell is got rid of with no trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Done cleanly means done smoothly and neatly, with no hitches or difficulty.

clue.text: Drive in river? Harrington's first round ending in torment

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the golfer's name is used
ending in means only the final letter of the following word is kept

blocks.note: the Tees is a river in north-east England
the initial letter of the name
O is round in shape
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: The golfer Padraig Harrington hits his opening drive into a river and his round ends in misery.
explanation.walkthrough: Padraig Harrington is an Irish golfer, which sets the golfing scene for the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive in golf is the long opening stroke played from the tee, which is exactly a tee shot.
